title: Brauer induction by one-dimensional subgroup representations
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a finite group. A finite-dimensional $F$-representation of $G$ is a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space with an action of $G$ by $F$-linear automorphisms. Write $R_F(G)$ for the abelian group generated by their isomorphism classes, with relations $[V\oplus W]=[V]+[W]$. For a subgroup $H\le G$ and a homomorphism $\lambda:H\to F^\times$, define $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G F_\lambda$ as the quotient of the $F$-vector space on symbols $e_g$ ($g\in G$) by $e_{gh}=\lambda(h)e_g$ for $g\in G$, $h\in H$, with action $a e_g=e_{ag}$. Then $R_F(G)$ is generated as an abelian group by the classes $[\operatorname{Ind}_H^G F_\lambda]$ as $H$ and $\lambda$ vary. Equivalently, every class in $R_F(G)$ is a finite linear combination of these classes with integer coefficients.

proof.text: Work first over $\mathbf C$. Put $\chi_V(g)=\operatorname{tr}(g\mid V)$. Trace on a block diagonal matrix is the sum of the traces, and trace is invariant under a change of basis, so $[V]\mapsto\chi_V$ defines an additive map $\chi:R_{\mathbf C}(G)\to\mathbf C^G$. By [lem-per-finite-group-character-decomposition], every virtual class is a finite sum $\sum_S a_S[S]$ over pairwise nonisomorphic irreducibles, with $a_S\in\mathbf Z$. Pairing $\chi(\sum a_S[S])$ with $\chi_T(g^{-1})$ using [lem-per-finite-group-character-orthogonality] gives the integer $a_T$ inside $\mathbf C$. Hence a zero character forces each $a_T=0$, and $\chi$ is injective. The two cited statements apply because the group is finite and the coefficient field $\mathbf C$ is algebraically closed by [lem-weil-complex-algebraically-closed] and of characteristic zero; Steps 2--4 work over this same field.

proof.text: Let $I\subseteq R_{\mathbf C}(G)$ be the additive subgroup spanned by $[\operatorname{Ind}_E^G W]$, for elementary subgroups $E$ and finite-dimensional $E$-representations $W$. The unit-character identity of [lem-per-brauer-elementary-unit-character] says that $\chi([\mathbf C])=\sum_i n_i\chi([\operatorname{Ind}_{E_i}^G W_i])$. By the injectivity just proved, $[\mathbf C]=\sum_i n_i[\operatorname{Ind}_{E_i}^G W_i]\in I$. This uses the theorem only for the unit character and arbitrary elementary-subgroup representations; no monomiality is assumed here.

proof.text:
The tensor identity and additivity in [lem-per-finite-group-induction-calculus] give
$$[V][\operatorname{Ind}_E^G W]=[\operatorname{Ind}_E^G(\operatorname{Res}_E^G V\otimes W)]\in I.$$
The right-hand representation is finite-dimensional. Distributing over sums and integer coefficients shows that $I$ is an ideal in the representation ring (multiplication is well-defined because tensor distributes over direct sums). Since $[\mathbf C]\in I$, every $[V]=[V][\mathbf C]$ lies in $I$. Explicitly,
$$[V]=\sum_i n_i[\operatorname{Ind}_{E_i}^G(\operatorname{Res}_{E_i}^G V\otimes W_i)].$$
Thus elementary induction generates all virtual classes. Frobenius reciprocity is part of the cited induction calculus; the ideal argument uses its representation-level tensor identity, rather than inferring that identity from reciprocity alone.

proof.text:
For each elementary $E$ and finite-dimensional $E$-representation $W$, use [lem-per-finite-group-character-decomposition] to write $W\simeq\bigoplus_j S_j$ with irreducible $S_j$ (no summands if $W=0$). The elementary-group clause of [lem-per-elementary-group-monomial] gives $S_j\simeq\operatorname{Ind}_{K_j}^{E}\mathbf C_{\lambda_j}$ for $K_j\leq E$. Additivity and transitivity from [lem-per-finite-group-induction-calculus] then give
$$[\operatorname{Ind}_E^G W]=\sum_j[\operatorname{Ind}_{K_j}^G\mathbf C_{\lambda_j}].$$
Substitute this into Step 3. All indices are finite, so multiplying their integer coefficients gives a finite integral combination of monomial classes. This proves the assertion over $\mathbf C$.

proof.text: Choose an algebraic closure $A$ of $\mathbf Q$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. By [lem-per-finite-group-algclosed-scalar-extension] applied to $L=\mathbf C$, algebraically closed by [lem-weil-complex-algebraically-closed], and to $L=F$, there are embeddings $i:A\hookrightarrow\mathbf C$ and $j:A\hookrightarrow F$, and ring isomorphisms $b_i,b_j$. Given $x\in R_F(G)$, set $y=b_j^{-1}(x)$ and apply Step 4 to $b_i(y)$. Every line character $\lambda:H\to\mathbf C^\times$ in that formula has a unique preimage $\lambda_A:H\to A^\times$ by the line-character bijection in the cited statement. Its induction comparison identifies the monomial class with $b_i([\operatorname{Ind}_H^G A_{\lambda_A}])$. Applying $b_i^{-1}$ and then $b_j$ therefore yields the same integral formula for $x$, with characters $j\lambda_A$ over $F$. This explicitly uses two embeddings from $A$; it requires no embedding $F\hookrightarrow\mathbf C$.

proof.text: The quotient induction used in [lem-per-finite-group-induction-calculus], specialized to the line $F_\lambda$, is exactly the quotient in the item: send $e_g$ to the class of $[g]\otimes1$, and send the class of $[g]\otimes a$ back to $a e_g$. The balancing relation is $[gh]\otimes1=[g]\otimes\lambda(h)=\lambda(h)([g]\otimes1)$, so both maps are well-defined and inverse. Both commute with left translation by every $a\in G$. Thus all generators in Step 5 are precisely the stated generators, with the stated sign of $\lambda$, and the claimed generation follows.
